o: Every prefix (first k digits) and suffix (last k digits) of num must be prime, including num itself. With num ≤ 10⁹ it has at most 10 digits, so there are ≤ 20 checks, each a trial-division primality test costing O(√num) ≈ 31623 divisions — trivially fast. Examples: 23 → prefixes {2,23}, suffixes {3,23} all prime → true; 39 fails immediately (39 = 3·13).
k: At most 10 prefixes and 10 suffixes; trial division suffices for 64-bit-range checks.

a.n: Approach 1: Trial Division on All Prefixes/Suffixes
a.i: Generate numeric prefixes by repeatedly stripping last digits; generate suffixes by taking num mod powers of ten; test each for primality.
s: isPrime(x): false for x < 2; test divisors up to √x.
For p = num; while p > 0: check p, then p //= 10.
For m = 10; while m / 10 <= num: check num % m; m *= 10.
a.t: O(D·√num) where D ≤ 10 is the digit count — about 3·10⁵ operations worst case

a.n: Approach 2: Sieve Small Primes + Trial Division
a.i: Precompute primes up to √(10⁹) ≈ 31623 with a sieve, then test each prefix/suffix by dividing only by those primes — a constant-factor speedup useful if num is queried many times.
s: Primality test divides candidate by each sieve prime up to its square root.
Run the same prefix/suffix loop with this test.
a.t: O(√num / ln√num) per test after O(√num) one-time sieving
a.sp: O(√num / ln√num) for the prime list

w: Plain trial division is plenty for a single call; the sieve pays off only with many queries. Pitfall: 1 is not prime (so num = 1 → false), and the suffix loop must include the full number itself. Follow-up: count complete primes below N (DFS over digit extensions).
